extracted.intended_audience: judges, patent litigators, and counsel preparing jury instructions in U.S. patent trials
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions and accompanying practice notes for adjudicating patent litigation issues (infringement, invalidity, claim construction, damages, willfulness, etc.) before a jury in U.S. courts. Designed to be customized to case-specific facts and legal issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims define patent scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The words of the claims define the scope of the patent owner’s exclusive rights during the life of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only the claims of the patent can be infringed; neither the written description nor the drawings can be infringed. Each claim must be considered individually and the same claim meaning must be used for infringement and invalidity analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Examiner considerations for patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: In examining a patent application, the Patent Examiner searches for prior art and considers whether each claim defines an invention that is new, useful, and not obvious, and whether claims are directed to eligible subject matter and are definite, enabled, and adequately described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the prosecution process and that prosecution history (file wrapper) may be relevant to claim interpretation and estoppel issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art (AIA vs pre-AIA) / Cutoff Date
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art is technical information against which patentability is judged; definitions vary under the AIA and pre-AIA. Under the AIA, prior art is knowledge publicly available before the effective filing date; pre-AIA definitions vary by subsection (§§ 102(a),(b),(d),(e),(g)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice Note: Model instructions refer to a 'Cutoff Date' which may differ by claim and pre-AIA subsection; juries may need instructions to determine differing Cutoff Dates and resulting pools of prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and standard of proof for invalidity
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is presumed valid, and the party challenging validity must prove invalidity by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice Note: Consider translating 'clear and convincing' to explanatory language such as 'highly probable' to aid juror understanding; the jury should be instructed on how this standard compares to preponderance and beyond a reasonable doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and standard of proof for infringement and other issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Issues such as infringement and damages are decided by a preponderance of the evidence (i.e., more likely than not).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The instructions distinguish this civil standard from the criminal 'beyond a reasonable doubt' standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction is the court’s role
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the judge’s job to interpret the meaning of claim language; jurors must accept the court’s claim constructions and use them for both infringement and invalidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For limitations not expressly construed by the court, jurors should apply the plain and ordinary meaning as understood by one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention (Teva/Phillips/Markman authority).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain and ordinary meaning / PHOSITA standard
rubrics_metrics.description: For claim limitations not construed by the court, use the plain and ordinary meaning as understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art (level of experience, education, training in the field) at the relevant time (pre-AIA: time of invention; AIA: before effective filing date).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model glossaries define 'ordinary skill in the art' differently for pre-AIA and AIA contexts. The jury may need guidance on establishing that skill level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function (35 U.S.C. § 112) construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Means[[step]]-plus-function claim limitations are limited to the corresponding structure (or act/step) described in the specification and equivalents thereof; the court determines the recited function and corresponding structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model language provides blanks for the recited function and corresponding structure; jurors must use the court's identification of corresponding structure when assessing infringement and validity of such limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal infringement requires every claim element
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is literally infringed only if the accused product or method includes each and every element (or method step) in that patent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infringement is assessed claim-by-claim. If even one claim element is missing, there is no literal infringement of that claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents (DOE)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim can be infringed under the doctrine of equivalents if the accused product/method contains an equivalent component/part/method step for each claimed element not literally present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that each missing claim element has an equivalent in the accused product; limitations on DOE include prosecution history estoppel and subject matter dedicated to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution history estoppel limits DOE
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecution history estoppel can limit application of the doctrine of equivalents where claim scope was narrowed or surrendered during prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Practice Notes and cited cases; jury should be instructed on whether prosecution history estoppel applies in the case at hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject matter dedicated to the public limits DOE
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter the patentee dedicated to the public (e.g., unclaimed disclosed subject matter) can limit application of the doctrine of equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury must be instructed about any dedication issues relevant to equivalence findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct infringement—knowledge and intent immaterial
rubrics_metrics.description: A party is liable for direct infringement if it made, used, imported, offered to sell, or sold the invention as defined by the claims during the patent term; knowledge of the patent and intent to infringe are immaterial to direct infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This instruction clarifies that intent or awareness of the patent is not required to establish direct infringement under § 271.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect infringement: inducement (active inducement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect infringement may occur if a defendant actively induces another to infringe a claim of the patent (induced infringement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model includes separate instructions (and Practice Notes) to distinguish induced infringement from contributory infringement and to lay out the elements the plaintiff must prove for inducement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect infringement: contributory infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant may be liable for contributory infringement for supplying a component especially made or adapted for use in a patented invention or for contributing to another’s infringement under certain statutory conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model instructions include treatment of contributory infringement and statutory sections applicable (e.g., §271(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement involving foreign supply and process-made products (§ 271(f), § 271(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: Special rules apply for infringement involving supply of all or a substantial portion of components to another country (§271(f)(1)), supplying components especially made for use overseas (§271(f)(2)), and import/sale/use of a product made by a patented process (§271(g)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model contains distinct instructions for §271(f)(1), §271(f)(2), and §271(g) situations; jury must be instructed on the statutory elements that apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation (novelty) and related prior-art doctrines
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipation requires that a single prior art reference (or earlier public disclosure) disclose every element of the claimed invention; the Model breaks out categories of prior art (prior public knowledge, public use, printed publication, prior patent, earlier-filed application, prior invention) and treats pre-AIA vs AIA distinctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple subsections (e.g., Prior Public Knowledge, Prior Public Use, On-Sale Bar, Printed Publication, Prior Patent, Earlier-Filed Patent Application, Prior Invention) provide detailed elements and fact patterns the jury must consider when deciding anticipation.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-sale bar and experimental use
rubrics_metrics.description: Bar to patentability can arise from on-sale activity; the Model separately addresses experimental use as a potential exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model distinguishes pre-AIA and AIA contexts and provides guidance on what constitutes an on-sale bar versus permissible experimental activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness (Graham factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness is decided using the four Graham factors: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between the claimed invention and the prior art; (3) level of ordinary skill in the art; and (4) secondary considerations (other considerations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model provides instructions for each factor and emphasizes the need to consider them collectively; examples and case citations are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination of the level of ordinary skill in the art is a fact question used in obviousness, claim construction, and other analyses; definitions vary slightly for pre-AIA vs AIA contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model includes definition language in the glossary and instructs juries on how that skill level informs claim meaning and obviousness analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement (35 U.S.C. §112)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must enable one of ordinary skill in the art to make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model provides a separate instruction on enablement and the jury’s role in assessing whether the specification meets the statutory enablement requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written-description requirement (35 U.S.C. §112)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must adequately describe the claimed invention to show that the inventor possessed the claimed subject matter at the time of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modeled as a distinct invalidity ground; jury instructed on how to evaluate adequacy of the written description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages—general principles and start date
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages are compensatory and may include various forms; model provides guidance on when damages begin (alternate instructions if start date is stipulated or disputed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury should be instructed on methods for calculating damages and the correct start date(s) depending on case facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages—kinds recoverable
rubrics_metrics.description: Types of damages that may be recovered include lost profits, price erosion, cost escalation, convoyed sales, and reasonable royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each damages category has its own instruction (e.g., lost profits methods, price erosion evidence, convoyed sales nexus). For reasonable royalty, multiple subtopics (comparable licenses, timing, multiple patents, availability of non-infringing substitutes) are covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty—factors and subtopics
rubrics_metrics.description: When awarding a reasonable royalty, the jury may consider evidence such as comparable license agreements, timing of the hypothetical negotiation, availability of acceptable non-infringing substitutes, the number of licenses needed (multiple patents), and other economic considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model cautions against hindsight and requires accounting for differences between actual licenses and the hypothetical negotiation; includes case citations (Georgia-Pacific and Federal Circuit guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Doubts regarding damages resolved against infringer
rubrics_metrics.description: Any doubts the jury may have on damages due to the defendant’s failure to keep proper records should be decided in favor of the plaintiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model cites precedent instructing juries to hold missing or confusing records against the defendant, not the plaintiff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard-Essential Patents (SEPs) and FRAND
rubrics_metrics.description: For SEPs, juries must be instructed on the particulars of any FRAND commitment, established patent law principles, and only those Georgia‑Pacific factors relevant to the case; royalties must be apportioned to the incremental value of the claimed invention, not the standard as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice Note: Emphasizes apportionment and limitation on irrelevant Georgia‑Pacific factors; cites Federal Circuit precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful infringement—general standard
rubrics_metrics.description: If the plaintiff proves infringement of a valid claim, the jury must determine whether the defendant’s infringement was willful by proving it is more likely than not that the defendant knew of the patent and intentionally infringed at least one asserted claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Willfulness requires consideration of the totality of the circumstances and assessment of defendant’s knowledge and intent at the time of the challenged conduct. A finding of willfulness should not directly affect the amount of damages awarded by the jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful infringement—reliance on legal opinion (35 U.S.C. §298)
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant may present reliance on counsel’s opinion as a factor in the willfulness analysis, but the AIA and subsequent technical corrections limit the use of failure to obtain an opinion as evidence of willfulness (35 U.S.C. §298).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model gives alternate instruction depending on whether defendant relies on an opinion; absent reliance, jurors are instructed not to infer unfavorable consequences from a defendant’s failure to obtain an opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of bracketed/stipulated language and glossaries for juror clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructions use bracketed terminology to allow find-and-replace customization for case-specific facts; parties should prepare a glossary of technical terms to distribute to jurors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice Notes: Brackets indicate where counsel should tailor instructions (e.g., [product]/[method], [the Plaintiff]/[the Defendant]); Practice Notes placed throughout provide non-law guidance to judges and counsel to improve juror comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial procedure and jury roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Model instructs jurors on the six phases of trial (jury selection, opening statements, evidence presentation, closing arguments, final instructions, deliberations) and clarifies that opening/closing statements are not evidence and jurors must base verdict on admitted evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice Note: Emphasize keeping an open mind as evidence is introduced piecemeal and following the judge’s legal instructions (including claim constructions) even if jurors disagree.
